$comment: THE SQLITE HARNESS LEG CATALOGUE — the declared, HOST-FREE answer to 'which targets does this harness build?'. D-HARNESS-CROSS-HOST-ANY-TARGET item (2). ★ THE RULE THIS FILE EXISTS TO ENFORCE: the set of legs is a property of the HARNESS, not of the machine running it. Read this file on Windows, on Linux, on an arm64 VPS or on a Mac and you get the SAME five legs. What the host changes is ONLY whether it can EXECUTE a leg's artifact — a separate question, answered by `runOn` + `launchers` below and never by an `if host == ...` in a driver. Before this file existed, build-and-test.sh derived its leg list from `uname` (pe64 was unreachable from any host, macho only from a Mac) and build-and-test.ps1 refused to start unless $IsWindows (pe64 was its ONLY leg, hardcoded). Each driver therefore conflated HOST with TARGET, which is the opposite of the user's hard requirement: 'build ANY target inside ANY host, this MUST work.'
$vocabularyComment: The declaration vocabulary is the CORPUS's, not a new one: `spec` and `runOn` mean exactly what they mean in examples/**/expected.json, and the verdicts a driver records for a leg come from the closed 7+1-name set in tests/test_support/arm_verdict_ledger.hpp (pinned by tests/harness/test_sqlite_harness_legs.cpp, which compares this catalogue's resolver output against that C++ enum). `launchers` is the ONE strict extension: the corpus's `emulator` key covers a cross-ARCH host on the SAME OS, and this harness additionally needs the cross-OS case (a pe64 artifact under Wine on Linux), so both are expressed as one ordered list of declared launchers keyed by (hostOs, hostArch). Absence of a matching launcher entry IS the 'none declared' declaration — there is no empty-string spelling, so a reader cannot mistake 'we looked and there is none' for 'nobody filled this in'. ★ EVERY launcher entry additionally declares `pathTranslation`: the PATH NAMESPACE its argv lives in, from the closed set in harness_legs.py (`none`, `windows-to-wsl`). It is required on every entry, never defaulted, for the same reason `zconfGuards` is: a reader must not have to know a default, and `none` — 'this launcher takes the driver's paths verbatim' — is a CLAIM about the launcher, not an absence. It exists because a launcher need not share a filesystem namespace with the driver that spawns it: `wine /home/me/x.exe` takes the driver's own path, `wsl.exe` needs `/mnt/c/...` where the driver holds a drive-letter path, and an untranslated path does not fail as a path error — the callee opens a relative file by that name, misses, and the run reads as a broken binary. The verb is resolved and APPLIED by harness_legs.py (`--translate-path` / `--assert-translated`), so the translator is named in one file and not in two drivers. ★★ AND `envTransfer`, THE SECOND HALF OF THE SAME FACT, found by measuring the first: a launcher in another OS namespace does not inherit the driver's ENVIRONMENT either. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-04 — a `wsl.exe`-launched fixture saw `SQLITE_TEST_PATTERN_LIST` and `QUICKTEST_OMIT` as EMPTY, so the corpus RESUME ENGINE (which selects its files through that variable) silently re-ran the corpus from the beginning instead of from the abort point: a harness that looks like it is working and is not. `inherit` = the child gets this driver's environment block (qemu, Wine, `arch`); `wslenv` = each variable must be NAMED in the `WSLENV` carrier. Resolved by harness_legs.py (`--env-transfer`), so the carrier and its separator are spelled once. ★★★ AND THE THIRD NAMESPACE, `runFilesystem`, FOUND THE SAME WAY THE SECOND WAS — BY MEASURING THE FIRST TWO AND FINDING THEM INSUFFICIENT [[D-HARNESS-WSL-LAUNCHED-LEG-RUNDIR-IS-DRVFS]]. `pathTranslation` says how a launcher SPELLS a path; `envTransfer` says whether it sees this driver's environment; NEITHER says which FILESYSTEM the launched process writes its databases onto — and the subject of this corpus is a database engine, so that is the one property it tests hardest. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-06 on this host, one process, two directories: `/mnt/c/…` (`9p … aname=drvfs`, **no `metadata` option**) answers `chmod 644` with **777** and `chmod 400` with **555**, because DrvFs derives the entire POSIX mode from the single Windows read-only ATTRIBUTE; `/tmp` (ext4) answers 644 and 400. ✔AND MEASURED BY A 2x2 MATCHED CONTROL ({DSS fixture, gcc reference} x {DrvFs rundir, ext4 rundir}, same staged corpus): **all 60 failures reproduce IDENTICALLY under the GCC REFERENCE on DrvFs and VANISH on ext4** — wal2 20, zipfile 12, e_walauto 10, journal3 8, attach 2, tkt3457 1, plus a `pager4` ABORT — i.e. ZERO of them are DSS-attributable. `driver` = the launched process writes where this driver writes (Wine's Z: mapping, qemu, `arch` — all one machine, one kernel, one filesystem); `wsl-linux` = the launcher crosses into a Linux kernel whose own filesystem is ext4 and which reaches this driver's files only through that compatibility mount. Required on EVERY entry, never defaulted, because `driver` is a CLAIM and it was the unexamined one. Resolved by harness_legs.py (`--run-dir-plan`), which also splices the launcher's working-directory option and hands back the argv prefixes that create/clear/populate the directory — so neither driver spells `--cd`, `mkdir`, `rm -rf` or `cp` for a foreign filesystem, and neither knows where in an argv an option has to go. ⛔ THE 60 FAILURES ARE NOT CONFOUNDS AND MUST NEVER BECOME ONE: the mechanism is ours and it is fixable, so a `confounds` row for them would launder a harness misconfiguration into 'expected' using the very mechanism that key exists to keep honest.
$confoundsComment: ★★ AN EARNED CONFOUND IS A PROPERTY OF THE LEG, NOT OF THE DRIVER YOU HAPPENED TO RUN [[D-HARNESS-CONFOUND-LEDGER-IS-PER-DRIVER-NOT-PER-LEG]], [[D-HARNESS-SQLITE-CONFOUNDS-NOT-DECLARED-PER-LEG]], [[D-SQLITE-CONFOUND-LIST-DRIVER-ASYMMETRY]]. A confound is a unit failure this harness has PROVEN is not the compiler's, by a matched control, on a named leg, on a named date — and since the count of GENUINE failures is what every verdict rests on, which failures are excused decides what this project believes about itself. Until this key existed the answer depended on WHICH DRIVER YOU RAN: `build-and-test.sh` read one global `DSS_CONFOUNDS` and applied it to EVERY leg including legs where nothing had ever been measured, while `build-and-test.ps1` returned an earned list for `pe64-x86_64` and an EMPTY one for everything else — and all six of its patterns had been earned on LINUX x86_64, so the Windows driver handed a Linux-earned list to the one leg that could not use it and withheld it from the legs that had earned it. ✔MEASURED CONSEQUENCE: the same elf64-x86_64 artefact's `zipfile-25.0` was a 'known non-DSS confound' under one driver and a 'genuine failure' under the other, in the same project on the same day, so no two legs' genuine-failure counts were comparable. ⇒ the declaration lives HERE, per leg, and every pattern carries `earnedOn` / `earnedAt` / `mechanism` / `anchor`; the lint REFUSES a pattern that does not show its work, refuses a duplicate, refuses one that does not compile as a regex, and refuses a missing key — because `[]` (nothing has ever been earned on this leg, every failure counts) is a CLAIM a catalogue has to make out loud, and a missing key could not be told from it. `scope` is the drivers' long-standing `native:`/`emulated:` vocabulary as a FIELD: `any` excuses however the leg runs, `native` only when this host executes the artefact directly, `emulated` only when it goes through a declared launcher. ⚠ THE OPERATOR OVERRIDE (`DSS_CONFOUNDS`) IS UNCHANGED AND STILL APPLIES TO EVERY LEG: an operator naming a pattern is stating intent for this run, not inheriting one, and both drivers announce which of the two is in force.
$noHostKeyingComment: NOTHING in this file may be keyed on the host. `build.libraries.searchPaths` is the one place host-shaped STRINGS appear, and they are CANDIDATES, not decisions: every path is tried on every host, a hit is used and a miss costs nothing. A driver that skips a search path because of the host it is on has reintroduced the defect. ⚠ If you are tempted to add a `"onlyOnHost"` key here, stop: the question you are answering is either 'can this host EXECUTE it' (that is `runOn`/`launchers`) or 'is a declared build input present' (that is a filesystem probe whose failure is the LOUD `skipped-build-input-missing` verdict) — never 'is this leg allowed to exist'.
$configureAnswersComment: ★★ AND THE SAME STORY ONE LAYER UP, FOR SQLITE'S OWN `./configure` (D-HARNESS-MACHO-LEG-INHERITS-THE-DERIVING-LINUX-HOSTS-CONFIGURE-PROBES). The recipe is derived by running `make -n` on the DERIVING host, and the ONE host-probe define left on that command line is `_HAVE_SQLITE_CONFIG_H` — which makes `sqliteInt.h` `#include "sqlite_cfg.h"`, and the include path points at the deriving host's build dir. So EVERY leg inherited THAT machine's ~52 configure answers wholesale. ✔MEASURED, the whole chain, on the macho64-arm64 CLI: the Linux `sqlite_cfg.h` sets `HAVE_PREAD64`/`HAVE_PWRITE64` → `os_unix.c` `#if defined(HAVE_PREAD64) && defined(HAVE_PWRITE64)` → `USE_PREAD64` → the `osPread64`/`osPwrite64` macros, typed with **`off64_t`** — a type Darwin does not have. `off64_t` + `pread64` + `pwrite64` are ONE defect, not three. ⛔ There is NO `HAVE_OFF64_T` macro anywhere in sqlite; the pe64 leg's `$recipeTransformComment` used to name one, and it never existed — that prose is corrected below. ★ THE CLASS IS CLOSED BY MACHINE DIFF, not by reasoning about the header: the deriving Linux `sqlite_cfg.h` against the Mac's OWN configure-generated one differ on EXACTLY THREE LINES — `HAVE_PREAD64`, `HAVE_PWRITE64`, `HAVE_MALLOC_H` — and all ~49 other answers (`HAVE_FDATASYNC`, `HAVE_GMTIME_R`, `HAVE_LOCALTIME_R`, `HAVE_USLEEP`, `HAVE_UTIME`, `HAVE_ISNAN`, `HAVE_NANOSLEEP`, `HAVE_REALPATH`, `HAVE_DLOPEN`, `HAVE_ZLIB`, the `HAVE_INT*_T` family, `SIZEOF_OFF_T 8`, …) are BYTE-IDENTICAL. That is why each leg declares THREE answers and not fifty: it declares only what `configure` actually VARIES across the targets this harness builds, and the deriving host answers the rest — correctly, because on those rows the two machines agree. Each leg's `build.configureAnswers` is REQUIRED, its values are real JSON booleans, and harness_legs.py's lint CROSS-CHECKS every one against the leg's own target (a Darwin leg declaring `HAVE_PREAD64: true` is refused, naming the evidence), so a wrong declaration fails the lint instead of shipping. The drivers then stage ONE `sqlite_cfg.h` per TARGET OS — the deriving host's answers for the identical rows, the leg's declared answers for the three that vary — into the harness's OWN cfg/ dir, placed AHEAD of the deriving host's build dir on the include list. `_HAVE_SQLITE_CONFIG_H` STAYS. ⚠ NOTE THE KEY IS THE TARGET OS AND NOT THE `recipeTransform`: four legs share `"none"` and they are TWO configurations (two Linux, two Darwin), so keying this on the transform would hand Darwin the Linux answers again — which is the defect. ⛔ TWO ALTERNATIVES WERE REJECTED, recorded because both are the obvious thing to reach for. (1) DERIVE THE RECIPE PER TARGET, on a machine of that target: that is what upstream's build system expects and it is why a native build never has this bug, but it makes the Darwin legs unbuildable on the four hosts out of five that are not a Mac — flatly the host-lock this file exists to end. (2) A BLUNT `darwin-selfconfig` TRANSFORM that just drops `_HAVE_SQLITE_CONFIG_H`, mirroring `windows-selfconfig`: ✔MEASURED to WORK, and still wrong — it discards ~49 CORRECT answers to fix 3 wrong ones, ~10 of them with real consequences (`HAVE_GMTIME_R`/`HAVE_LOCALTIME_R` fall back to the NON-REENTRANT `gmtime`/`localtime` in a SQLITE_THREADSAFE=1 build; `HAVE_FDATASYNC` becomes `#define fdatasync fsync`; `HAVE_USLEEP` drops sqlite3_sleep to 1-SECOND granularity, which the timing-sensitive corpus WILL notice). The same blunt drop is acceptable on WINDOWS only because `SQLITE_OS_WIN` re-configures the whole `os_win.c` path and none of those Unix answers is consulted there.
$stagedHeadersComment: ★ THE THIRD-PARTY HEADERS A LEG COMPILES AGAINST ARE A TARGET FACT, NOT A HOST ONE (D-HARNESS-SQLITE-STAGE-ZCONF-IS-PE-SHAPED, closed TF-C115). The staged zlib header is copied from the DERIVING POSIX host, where `./configure` baked ITS OWN probe results into zconf.h — `#if 1 → #define Z_HAVE_UNISTD_H` and friends. Those are facts about the deriving machine, exactly like the recipe's HAVE_*/Z_HAVE_* defines that `recipeTransform` exists to drop, and handing them to a foreign target is the same cross-compile category error one level down. Each leg therefore DECLARES `build.zconfGuards` — the value ITS target has for each guard `./configure` may have set — and the drivers stage ONE zinc/ PER `recipeTransform` (stage-zinc.py, called by both) and give each leg an include list pointing at its own. Two legs may share a zinc/ only by sharing a recipeTransform, and the lint refuses a catalogue where same-transform legs declare different guards. Before this, ONE pe-shaped zinc/ served every leg and the .ps1 REFUSED (`poisoned`) any leg that was not `windows-selfconfig` rather than compile it against the wrong header — the right call, and the reason this key exists is to make the refusal unnecessary instead of relaxing it.
$loadExtHelperBuilderComment: ★★★ THE COMPILER THIS REPOSITORY SHIPS BUILDS THE CORPUS'S dlopen()ed HELPER — NO HOST NEEDS A THIRD-PARTY CROSS-COMPILER FOR ANY LEG. Operator, 2026-08-05: 'why do we need mingw? since dss code prime should not have dependencies?' / 'I installed mingw in wsl, but we should NOT depend on a tool'. The `$targetCcComment` below is still TRUE and its rule is unchanged — a compiler's name is not a declaration of its target — but the SHAPE it left behind made every leg's RUN conditional on this machine owning a cross-compiler for that leg's target (a mingw gcc for pe64, aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc for the arm64 leg, an Apple clang for the two macho legs), and a leg without one recorded `skipped-build-input-missing` and did not run its ~330,000 units. That is the same host-lock D-HARNESS-CROSS-HOST-ANY-TARGET exists to end, one layer down from the fixture. ⇒ each leg now DECLARES `build.sharedLibFormat` and DSS emits the helper for it. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-05 on this project's WINDOWS box — one host, all five legs, rc=0 and zero diagnostics on every one: pe64 8,704 B · elf64-x86_64 13,912 B · elf64-aarch64 13,912 B · macho64-arm64 67,426 B · macho64-x86_64 17,890 B. The three a machine here can LOAD were loaded THROUGH SQLITE'S OWN `sqlite3_load_extension()` (dlopen + dlsym `testloadext_init`, exactly what test/loadext.test does) and `SELECT half(9.0)` returned 4.500 — pe64 natively on Windows, elf64-x86_64 in WSL, elf64-aarch64 under qemu-aarch64; the loading program was built by the REFERENCE compiler each time, so the only thing under test was the DSS artefact. ★ THE CONTROL IS KEPT, DELIBERATELY, BECAUSE DSS IS NOW TESTING DSS: a defect SHARED by the fixture and the helper (both compile sqlite3ext.h) could cancel and read as green. So wherever a VERIFIED target compiler happens to exist, the same source is ALSO built with it and both artefacts are reported side by side — never gating, never staging — and `DSS_LOADEXT_HELPER=reference` STAGES the control instead, which makes the corpus itself the differential. There is NO automatic fallback: a DSS emission failure is a compiler defect and this harness exists to surface them, so it is `poisoned` with the diagnostics quoted, never quietly rebuilt another way.
$targetCcComment: ★★ A COMPILER'S NAME IS NOT A DECLARATION OF ITS TARGET, and this catalogue once said it was. ⚠ READ `$loadExtHelperBuilderComment` FIRST: since 2026-08-05 this key governs the optional CONTROL arm, not a required build input — a leg whose `targetCc` resolves to nothing on this host still builds its helper (with DSS) and still runs its corpus. D-HARNESS-LOADEXT-HELPER-TARGET-BLINDNESS-NOW-ABORTS-THE-RUN. `build.targetCc.candidates` is a list of names to TRY, in order; it is NOT a list of compilers that are known to build this leg. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-05 on a WSL/Ubuntu x86_64 host: both elf legs ran GREEN (6 err / 331,351 and 5 err / 331,355, all known confounds) and the run then DIED in /usr/bin/ld — 'relocation R_X86_64_PC32 against symbol `sqlite3_api` can not be used when making a shared object; recompile with -fPIC' — building the pe64 leg's loadext helper, and pe64's units never ran. The mingw cross-compiler was absent, this leg listed plain `gcc` as an ALTERNATIVE, and so a LINUX compiler was picked, legitimately, to build a WINDOWS shared object. build-and-test.sh:2615 and :3804 both forbid exactly that fallback in so many words; neither guard fired, because the config had already licensed what the guards were watching for. ⇒ THE RESOLVER NOW ASKS THE COMPILER. harness_legs.py `--resolve-target-cc <leg>` accepts a candidate only if `<cc> -dumpmachine` names this leg's own target arch AND target OS, both derived from the leg's declared `spec`. No new key, because the leg already declares its target; no host test; no format-name branch. A candidate that CANNOT state its target (the probe fails) is REFUSED, never assumed — the leg is still BUILT, it records `skipped-build-input-missing`, and its corpus does not run. ★ AND THE RULE IS NOT pe64-SHAPED: the elf64-x86_64 leg's `cc`/`gcc`/`clang` resolve to an aarch64 compiler on this project's native arm64 Linux VPS, which is the wrong-arch helper D-HARNESS-ARM64-LEG-HOST-ARCH-HELPER-SO is named after; the same one check refuses it. ★★ WHAT IT BUILDS is the corpus's dlopen()ed helper extension, whose FILE NAME is also a target fact — see each leg's `loadExtHelperName`.
$stageBuildComment: ★★★ WHICH SQLITE THE CORPUS IS ACTUALLY TESTING — DECLARED ONCE, FOR EVERY LEG AND BOTH DRIVERS. Operator, 2026-08-06: 'yes, we need tests with the fts5 and other extensions enabled too'. ✔MEASURED on the elf64-x86_64 corpus.log of 2026-08-06: 362 of the 1,241 files the run reported as COMPLETED asserted NOTHING — they emitted only the two teardown lines every file emits (`<f>.test-closeallfiles... Ok`, `<f>.test-sharedcachesetting... Ok`) and returned at their first `ifcapable` gate (`fts5aa.test:19  ifcapable !fts5 { finish_test; return }`). The capability histogram over that inert set: fts5 110 files · fts3 86 · session 37 · rtree 27 · stat4 14 · then a long tail. ⚠ THE COMPILER WAS ALREADY COMPILING THE CODE THOSE FILES WOULD HAVE TESTED — `fts5.c`, `fts5_tcl.c`, `fts5_test_mi.c` and `fts5_test_tok.c` were 4 of the 189 TUs, preprocessed down to nothing. So the run paid to compile and to load every one of them and got no coverage back, and a headline of '1,241 files completed' counted all 362. ⇒ THE CAPABILITY SET IS NOW A DECLARATION, not a per-driver accident. ★ WHY THESE FLAGS AND NOT A SET I INVENTED: `--enable-all` is UPSTREAM'S OWN aggregate (configure --help: 'Enable these extensions: fts4 fts5 rtree geopoly session dbpage dbstat carray'), and it is the spelling sqlite's own test matrix uses — test/testrunner_data.tcl `build(All-O0)`, `build(All-Debug)`, `build(Sanitize)`. The rest are the flags upstream's own richest configurations add on top (`Check-Symbols`, `Debug-One`, `Update-Delete-Limit`). ⚠ `--memsys3` IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT: ✔MEASURED — configure accepts it, exits 0, and emits NO define, because MEMSYS5 wins. A declared flag that silently does nothing is the same defect as an undeclared one, so it is not declared. That is also exactly what `requiredDefines` exists to catch on every future run. ★ `optionDefines` is a SEPARATE MECHANISM because upstream offers no configure flag for these: main.mk's `OPT_FEATURE_FLAGS = … $(OPTIONS)` is the documented client knob and it is passed on the MAKE command line. ✔MEASURED: `OPTS=` handed to configure lands in the Makefile but NEVER on a testfixture compile line, while `make OPTIONS=-DSQLITE_ENABLE_STAT4` reached 106 of them.

stageBuild.$comment: Consumed by build-and-test.sh AND build-and-test.ps1 through `harness_legs.py --stage-build`. Neither driver spells any of it out: a capability enabled in one driver and not the other is this project's canonical silent harness bug, and it had ALREADY HAPPENED here — the sqlite3 CLI recipe carried -DSQLITE_ENABLE_FTS4 -DSQLITE_ENABLE_RTREE while the testfixture recipe built from the SAME tree carried neither, so 'which extensions exist' had two answers inside one run.
stageBuild.$requiredDefinesComment: THE FAIL-LOUD LINK between a flag and its effect. Every name here MUST appear in the -D set the harness derives from `make -n`, or the run DIES before compiling anything. This is not belt-and-braces: a configure flag can be accepted and do nothing (`--memsys3`, measured above), upstream can rename or retire a flag, and either way the corpus would go on reporting files as 'completed' while asserting nothing — which is the exact failure this whole block exists to end. Derived by MEASUREMENT from the OPT_FEATURE_FLAGS that these flags produced, never assumed from their names.
stageBuild.$capabilityWitnessesComment: AFTER the corpus runs, each capability's witness file must have emitted at least ONE non-teardown result. `requiredDefines` proves the define reached the COMPILER; a witness proves the capability reached the TESTS, which is the property the operator actually asked for. ★ Every witness was chosen from the MEASURED inert set and has exactly ONE decisive gate, so it is red today and turns green by this change — the red-on-disable demonstration is a property of the declaration rather than a separate experiment. A file with two gates would stay inert for a capability this set does NOT enable and report the gate red for the wrong reason; that is why `fts4aa` (gates `!fts3` + `fts4_deferred`) was not used, and why fts4/geopoly/column_metadata have no witness at all and rest on `requiredDefines` alone. ⚠ `define` IS DECLARED RATHER THAN DERIVED FROM THE CAPABILITY NAME, and the self-test found out why: the pair `mem5` ↔ `SQLITE_ENABLE_MEMSYS5` shares no substring, so the obvious structural check ('the capability name appears inside its define') fails on a perfectly correct row. A heuristic that has to be weakened to accept real data is worth less than the explicit pairing it was trying to avoid writing. ★★ **VET A WITNESS FOR *ANY* EARLY RETURN, NOT JUST FOR `ifcapable` — MEASURED THE HARD WAY 2026-08-07.** The first vetting pass grepped only `ifcapable` and declared `mem5` single-gated. It is not: `test/mem5.test:26` also exits on `if {[info exists ::G(perm:presql)]} { finish_test; return }`, a PERMUTATION gate with nothing to do with the capability — and the first real run duly reported `mem5.test` inert while `SQLITE_ENABLE_MEMSYS5` sat in the recipe at line 17 of 35. That is a gate going red for a reason its capability cannot fix, which is worse than no witness at all, so `mem5` was REMOVED (the define-level check still proves MEMSYS5 compiled in). `analyze3` was replaced by `analyze6` for the same reason — `analyze3.test:31` exits on a `[permutation]` equality test against the `prepare` permutation. The surviving witnesses have exactly one exit in their preamble; `rtree1` and `session1` also carry the boilerplate `if {![info exists testdir]}` source-guard, which sets a variable rather than returning.
stageBuild.$scanstatusComment: ⛔ `--scanstatus` IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT, and it is the one capability this harness cannot currently ask for. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-07, TF-C132, by running it: `SQLITE_ENABLE_STMT_SCANSTATUS` is one of the three macros that make `src/vdbe.c:27-30` include `src/hwtime.h`, whose line 43 is GNU EXTENDED inline assembly — `__asm__ __volatile__ ("rdtsc" : "=a" (lo), "=d" (hi));`. DSS parses neither the `__volatile__` alternate spelling (`error[P0009]: expected 'ParenOpen' or 'VolatileKeyword' — got '__volatile__'`) nor the `:` operand lists, and the parser then desynchronises through the rest of vdbe.c: 54 errors on the fixture and 54 on the CLI, every one of them in vdbe.c / hwtime.h / vdbeInt.h and NONE anywhere else — so this flag was the whole blocker and the other eleven capabilities compile clean. It buys exactly TWO test files (scanstatus, scanstatus2). ⚠ It is NOT dropped because it is unimportant: upstream's own `build(Default)` in test/testrunner_data.tcl carries `-DSQLITE_ENABLE_STMT_SCANSTATUS`, so DSS cannot yet build sqlite's DEFAULT configuration. That is a compiler gap with its own anchor — [[D-LANG-GNU-EXTENDED-INLINE-ASM-UNSUPPORTED]] — not a harness decision to be quietly re-litigated here. Re-add the flag in the same change that closes it; `requiredDefines` will then prove it took.

legs.label: elf64-x86_64
legs.$launchersComment: qemu-x86_64 lets an arm64 Linux host run this leg. ★ NOTE THE ASYMMETRY WITH THE CORPUS, which is a finding and not a copy error: examples/**/expected.json declares NO emulator on its (x86_64, linux) arms, so on the native arm64 Linux VPS every one of them is a structural skip even though qemu-x86_64 exists. This catalogue declares it; the corpus's omission is tracked separately (D-TEST-CORPUS-NO-QEMU-X86_64-ON-ARM64-HOST). ★★ `wsl.exe` IS THE SECOND ENTRY AND IT CLOSES D-HARNESS-NO-WSL-LAUNCHER-FOR-ELF-ON-WINDOWS. A Windows host BUILDS this leg (TF-C115 did) and could always have RUN it — the artefact built by build-and-test.ps1 passed 330,436 tests under WSL BY HAND — but nothing declared the launcher, so the driver recorded `skipped-by-runOn` beside a binary it had just produced. It is not a plain command entry: wsl.exe lives in a DIFFERENT PATH NAMESPACE from the driver that spawns it (`pathTranslation`) AND in a different ENVIRONMENT namespace (`envTransfer`). The second was found by measuring the first — with paths translated but the environment assumed to inherit, the corpus resume engine's file selection arrived EMPTY and the resume re-ran the whole corpus while looking like it worked. ★★★ AND THE THIRD NAMESPACE, WHICH IS THE ARGV ITSELF: the command is `wsl.exe -e`, and this entry said `wsl.exe --` until 2026-08-04. `--` is documented as 'pass the remaining command line as is' and it is NOT the same as `-e`/`--exec` — ✔MEASURED on this host, one variable changed: `wsl.exe -- /nope` answers `/bin/bash: line 1: /nope: No such file` while `wsl.exe -e /nope` answers `execvpe(/nope) failed`, i.e. `--` reconstructs a command LINE and feeds it to the distro's DEFAULT SHELL. That shell then expands the fixture's argv a second time — MEASURED, a single argument `/mnt/c/.../g/*.test` came back to the callee as TWO arguments under `--` and as one under `-e`, and `$`, backticks, `;` and the backslash escape are live there too. A launcher whose argv is silently re-parsed cannot be trusted to have run the file the driver named, which is the same class of defect as an untranslated path. Recorded as D-TOOLS-WSL-EXE-WITHOUT-DASH-E-RUNS-A-LOCAL-SHELL and pinned by tests/harness/test_sqlite_harness_legs.cpp.
legs.$confoundsComment: See the top-level $confoundsComment. THIS IS THE LEG EVERY MATCHED CONTROL IN THE PROJECT WAS RUN ON — the DSS fixture and a gcc-built full-source REFERENCE testfixture, same box, same sqlite tree, same libtcl8.6.so — so it is the only leg whose rows are earned by a compiler-vs-compiler experiment rather than by observation. ⚠ THE FIRST FOUR ARE ONE DEFECT WEARING FOUR NAMES: this host's CLOCK_REALTIME oscillates between two values ~34.47 s apart, flipping every ~5 s (two instruments, 49 and 48 steps, spread 35.164 s), and every wall-clock assertion in the corpus reads its number from Tcl's `time`, which lives entirely outside DSS-compiled code. build.$sharedLibFormatComment: ★ THE FILE NAME AND THE FORMAT DISAGREE ON THIS TARGET, AND BOTH ARE RIGHT. The declared `loadExtHelperName` below is `libtestloadext.so` — sqlite's own choice, MEASURED, see its comment — while the object format is a `dylib`. DSS emits `<stem>.dylib` and the driver STAGES it under the name the corpus looks for; the extension in a Mach-O file's name has never been what makes it loadable. ✔MEASURED 2026-08-05 from a Windows host: 67,426 bytes, `Mach-O 64-bit arm64 dynamically linked shared library, flags:<NOUNDEFS|DYLDLINK|TWOLEVEL|NO_REEXPORTED_DYLIBS>`. ⚠ It has NOT been LOADED — there is no off-Mac loader for it, which is the same structural fact this leg's empty `launchers` list already declares. build.$loadExtHelperNameComment: The `.so` spelling, on a Darwin target, is NOT a copy error. ✔MEASURED at test/loadext.test:26-32: the name is chosen from `tcl_platform(platform)` (`unix` on a Mac), and the `tcl_platform(os) eq Darwin` branch three lines down changes only the COMPILER FLAGS (`-dynamiclib`, which is what this leg's sharedLibFlags already say) — never the file name.
build.$librariesComment: ★ THIS LEG ACQUIRES ITS LIBRARIES (D-HARNESS-LIBRARY-ACQUISITION-BUILT-FOR-ONE-LEG-IN-ONE-DRIVER). It used to declare `host-system`, which on any non-Mac means 'hope this box has a Darwin libtcl' — i.e. it never built anywhere but a Mac, in flat contradiction of the harness's own contract that every leg is BUILT everywhere and only RUN is gated. Anchor D-FF1-MACHO-FAT.` — and handed the thin arm64 slice OF THE SAME FILE it succeeds with rc=0. So slicing is the contract that anchor states, performed here because the harness is the only layer that knows which arch this leg wants (`readImports(path, reporter)` takes no target). ⚠ THE REFUSAL'S SPELLING CHANGED INSIDE THIS CYCLE, and the first draft of this comment quoted the older one: `guessFormat` read the fat magic little-endian, so a real universal binary could never reach the arm above and fell into the unknown-magic catch-all instead — the anchor's own remediation was unreachable. That detection bug was fixed in the same cycle; the quote above is the post-fix message. ★ Slicing would be right even if DSS read fat files: a leg's build input should be a library FOR THAT LEG'S TARGET, not a container that also holds a foreign architecture, or 'which architecture did this leg resolve against?' has no answer from the input.
libraries.$importNameComment: ★★ THE TRAP, AND WHY THE ANSWER IS `@loader_path` AND NOT A SYSTEM PATH. Both archives' LC_ID_DYLIB reads `/opt/local/lib/…` (✔MEASURED: `/opt/local/lib/libtcl8.6.dylib`, `/opt/local/lib/libz.1.dylib`), and DSS records a resolved library's EMBEDDED identity as the LC_LOAD_DYLIB — so linking naively produces a Mach-O that demands MacPorts at that prefix on the target Mac. That is a dyld LOAD failure, not a build error, so nothing on this host would catch it. The obvious fix is to record the system path instead — and this project cannot HONESTLY do that for Tcl: nobody here has measured what a Mac carries at /usr/lib for Tcl 8.6, and this repo's own darwin path installs Tcl through Homebrew, whose current `tcl-tk` is 9.x — so `/usr/lib/libtcl8.6.dylib` would be an unverified claim about someone else's machine, and a wrong one costs a dyld failure. `@loader_path/<name>` is TRUE BY CONSTRUCTION: dyld resolves it against the directory holding the executable, the driver stages the acquired dylib there beside the artefact, and the result assumes NOTHING about the target Mac's prefix layout or Tcl version. ⚠ For zlib a system path WOULD be defensible — this harness has measured that `/usr/lib/libz.1.dylib` resolves out of the dyld shared cache even though it cannot be opened as a file (see build-and-test.sh's darwin branch) — but mixing the two policies inside one artefact buys nothing and makes the rule harder to state. The acquired dylib bakes in `/opt/local/lib/tcl8.6` — MacPorts' own prefix — and MacPorts is not installed on that Mac; only the dylib was ever downloaded. ⇒ the SAME pinned archive also carries the scripts (✔MEASURED: 225 files, 4 subdirectories, ZERO symlinks under `opt/local/lib/tcl8.6/`, 1,948,034 bytes, `init.tcl` among them), so they are staged from it, pinned by a whole-tree digest, and handed to the drivers as `scriptLibraryDir` for TCL_LIBRARY. ⛔ NOT the host's Homebrew `tcl-tk@8` scripts: that works on ONE Mac, reintroduces exactly the host-dependence this arc exists to end, and pairs an 8.6.18 script library with a MacPorts 8.6.17 binary on nothing but a version-number coincidence.

The remaining 10 are here. Exactly ONE is runtime data, and it is the one that cost the corpus.

the manual page directory, from the same tclConfig.sh block. No code path in a Tcl interpreter reads it.
